title: Detection of Artificial Intelligence
summary: This detection strategy targets the resource development sub technique of obtaining artificial intelligence capabilities, where an adversary buys, licenses, or builds artificial intelligence tools and models for later use in an operation. It matters because those tools improve the wording of phishing messages, generate code, and automate parts of an intrusion, which raises the success rate of later stages. The telemetry that makes detection possible is cloud service audit and application programming interface logs for artificial intelligence services, endpoint process and file creation records for local model files, and network records for large uploads or downloads. The main failure mode is that most artificial intelligence use is legitimate business work, so a rule that alerts on the technology itself is pure noise and must instead focus on unsanctioned providers, unusual data volume, and model files.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that someone is getting artificial intelligence tools or models. The person may buy them or build them. Artificial intelligence, or AI, means software that can write text, images, or code by itself. The rule looks at company accounts and devices where these tools or models are used.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers use AI to write messages that are hard to notice as fake. They also use it to work faster and to try more targets. When you see the tool arrive early, you have time to stop the later steps. It also helps you find company data that staff send to tools nobody approved.
howItWorks: Cloud audit logs record every call to an AI service from a company account.
The rule checks the service name against the list of providers the company allows.
It counts the size and number of requests in a short window for each account.
Endpoint records show when a large model file is written to a device.
Proxy logs show uploads of large text or source files to an AI provider.
A request to a provider that is not approved, or a very large model download, raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a workshop that keeps a tool inventory list. Every new power tool gets a line with the buyer name and the date. A tool that appears on the list without a purchase order gets a question from the manager. The same is true for a costly tool bought on a personal card. The AI service calls are those lines in the inventory.
takeaways: Alert on unsanctioned providers and unusual volumes, not on AI use in general.
Cloud service audit logs and endpoint model file records are the main evidence.
A data loss angle matters as much as the tool itself, because staff may paste sensitive text.

objectives: Define artificial intelligence capability acquisition in the resource development phase.
Name the cloud and endpoint records that show AI service or model use.
Build a rule that compares observed AI providers against an approved list.
Explain how request volume and file size separate benign use from abuse.
Describe the limits of detection when a model runs on a personal device.
dataSources: Cloud service audit logs recording calls to approved and unsanctioned artificial intelligence model endpoints with request size and identity
Secure web gateway or proxy logs showing uploads of large text or source code files to generative service domains
Endpoint file creation records for large model weight files written into user profile directories
Endpoint process creation records for local inference runtimes and agent frameworks launched by standard user accounts
logic: The pattern is a company identity using an artificial intelligence service that is not on the approved provider list, or moving unusually large volumes of text and code to such a service, or pulling model weight files onto an endpoint that has no approved artificial intelligence workload. The fields that must be correlated are the calling identity, the destination service or domain, the request or file size, the destination device, and the time of day. The malicious case is an unapproved provider used with large payloads, or a model download on a host outside the data science group, especially combined with later outbound beaconing. The benign case is an approved provider, a small prompt, and a user inside the team that the company has already authorised for this work.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Unsanctioned Artificial Intelligence Service Use With Large Payload
# logsource:
#   product: aws
#   service: cloudtrail
# detection:
#   selection:
#     eventName|startswith:
#       - 'InvokeModel'
#       - 'GetModel'
#   filter_approved:
#     requestParameters.modelId|contains:
#       - 'approved-internal-'
#       - 'corp-'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Data science teams pulling approved open model weights onto research workstations
Marketing staff who paste long campaign drafts into a consumer chat tool that the company later approves
Software build jobs that download a language model for code review tooling on a development server
tuningNotes: Build an inventory of approved artificial intelligence providers and internal model endpoints first, then filter on that list and scope the rule to managed identities outside the research group. Add request and file size thresholds based on a two week baseline per team, and keep a separate, quieter record of all provider use for review. The coverage you lose is a small, careful use of an unapproved tool that stays below the size threshold, and none of this rule helps if a model runs entirely on a personal device outside management.
